display.title: Tanya Shiur 49: Chapter 36, Why Hashem Wants a Home in This Lowly World
display.summary_short: A Yiddish Tanya class: the Zohar's parable of the lamp from chapter 35, then the opening of chapter 36, on why Hashem desired a dwelling in this lowest world and what 'lower' means.
display.summary_long: Shiur 49 in Rabbi Yosef Goldstein's Yiddish Tanya series, the second side of a tape. It reviews chapter 35: the Zohar's parable of a lamp, which needs a wick, oil and a flame. Torah study in thought and speech draws the Shechinah onto the soul, but only a mitzvah done in action, the oil, brings it down to the body and the animal soul. Chapter 36 then asks why Hashem created the worlds. Each higher world exists for the one below it, so this lowest world is the purpose of them all. The rabbi surveys reasons given in Chassidic discourses, from Etz Chaim and the Zohar, and explains the Midrash that Hashem desired a dwelling below. A dwelling is where the owner himself lives, and the mezuzah shows that a Jewish home belongs to Hashem. Since there is no above or below before Hashem, 'lower' means a place where G-dliness is most hidden. The class ends with the Mitteler Rebbe's parable of the king who was moved only by a little bird that called out 'Long live the king!', because something new and unexpected brings true pleasure.
display.lesson: Hashem's deepest pleasure comes from the physical mitzvos a Jew does in this lowly world, which turn it into His home.
